transcript.text:
The missing number is 4, so:
2/3 = 4/6

How to solve it:
Look at the denominators (the bottom numbers): to get from 3 to 6, you multiply by 2 (3 × 2 = 6).
Do the exact same thing to the numerator (the top number): multiply 2 by 2 (2 × 2 = 4).
I do not understand why you multiply. Why do you use two?

Think of a fraction like a pizza.

The bottom number (denominator) is how many total slices the pizza is cut into.
The top number (numerator) is how many slices you get.

In the first fraction, 2/3, the pizza is cut into 3 big slices, and you have 2 of them.

Now, imagine you take a knife and cut every single slice right down the middle into 2 smaller pieces:
Your 3 total slices double to become 6 total slices (3 × 2 = 6).
Your 2 slices also double to become 4 smaller slices (2 × 2 = 4).

You didn't get any extra pizza—the pieces are just half as big, so you have twice as many of them.

We use 2 specifically because 6 is 2 times bigger than 3. To keep the amount of pizza completely fair and equal, whatever you do to the bottom number, you must do the exact same thing to the top number.

Want to try a quick practice problem together to test this out?

It is actually 4/6, not 2/6. Here is why 2/6 is different:

Imagine that pizza cut into 6 smaller slices:
2/6 means you only get 2 of those smaller slices. Since the slices are half the size of the original ones, 2/6 is actually only half as much pizza as 2/3.
4/6 means you get 4 of those smaller slices, which adds up to the exact same amount of pizza as 2 big slices (2/3).

Because the bottom number doubled from 3 to 6, your slices have to double from 2 to 4 to keep it equal.

Want to try another one, like finding what 1/2 equals out of 8?
I no understand pizza. Why bottom number go big, but top number must go big too?

Forget the pizza—think about money instead.

Imagine 1 is made of 3 big coins.
If you have 2 of those big coins, you have 2/3.

Now, imagine you trade each big coin for 2 smaller coins:
The whole 1 is now made of 6 small coins (that is the bottom number).
If you kept only 2 small coins (2/6), you would lose half your money!
To keep the exact same amount of money, your 2 big coins must also turn into 4 small coins (4/6).

Why both numbers grow:
When the pieces get smaller (the bottom number goes up), you need more of them (the top number goes up) just to keep the same amount you started with.

Want me to show this with a simple drawing using bars?
I understand money, but I no get why bottom number go from three to six.

The bottom number went from 3 to 6 only because the math problem asked for it.

Look back at your very first message: 2/3 = ?/6

Whoever wrote the question put the 6 there as a puzzle for you to solve. It didn't change from 3 to 6 on its own—the question is basically asking:
"If we force the bottom number to be 6 instead of 3, what does the top number have to be so the value stays fair?"

Because the question picked 6, we look at how 3 gets to 6 (multiply by 2). If the question had picked 9 (2/3 = ?/9), we would have multiplied by 3 instead!

Want to try solving one where the question picks a different bottom number, like 2/3 = ?/9?
Is 4/6 because three times two is six and two times two is four. next: 2/9 + 4/9?

You nailed it! That is the exact right logic for 4/6.

Now for your next problem: 2/9 + 4/9

The answer is 6/9 (which can also be simplified to 2/3).

How to solve it:
Check the bottom numbers: They are already the same (9 and 9). When the bottom numbers match, you do not add them together—the bottom number stays 9 because the size of the pieces hasn't changed.
Add the top numbers: Just add how many pieces you have: 2 + 4 = 6.
So you get 6/9.

(Bonus: Notice that 6 and 9 can both be divided by 3, which brings you right back to 2/3—the exact fraction you started with!)

Want to try adding two fractions where the bottom numbers are different?
